source: Mohammadirad, Masoud. 2026. A grammar of Hewramî. Language Science Press.
claim: The description is based primarily on 46 narratives collected during fieldwork in 2016–2023, supplemented by elicitation; chapter 3 treats phonetics, phonology and morphophonology.
The consonant inventory contains 29 consonant phonemes; four are peripheral phonemes restricted to a few loans or limited syllable/word distributions.
Table 2.1 gives p b t d k ɡ q (ʔ), t͡ʃ d͡ʒ, m n (ŋ), f s z ʃ ʒ x (γ) ħ ʕ h, ɾ r l (ɫ), w j; parenthesized phonemes are peripheral.

claim: The grammar analyzes nine phonemic vowels, distinguished by height/backness and phonetic realization: front /i e ɛ/ plus a front vowel represented <e> with [ɛ~æ], back /u o ɑ/, and central /ɨ ʊ/.

claim: The source characterizes /i e ɛ u ɑ o/ and [ɛ~æ] as long, while central /ɨ/ and /ʊ/ are short.
A Hewramî syllable minimally contains a vowel and maximally has two consonants on each side, yielding (C)(C)V(C)(C).
Consonant clusters that violate syllable structure are broken up by epenthetic i or u depending on the quality of adjacent consonants.

Stress placement is lexically/grammatically contrastive despite broad predictability by category; for most present-tense verbs stress alone distinguishes indicative from subjunctive (e.g. beró vs béro).
Masculine nouns generally follow final stress; feminine nouns generally have penultimate stress except nouns ending in stressed ê; past-tense verbal categories are likewise generally penultimate.
/w/ is usually realized [v] syllable-initially, more often [w] syllable-finally, and may lenite intervocalically to [ʋ].

In CCV onsets the first consonant is generally an obstruent and the second is often a sonorant (liquid, approximant, or nasal); CCVC is also attested when the second onset consonant is an approximant.
CVCC and CCVCC are permitted; coda clusters usually have a sibilant or approximant first and an obstruent second.
